newArguments.title: Correlated-evidence sensitivity test
newArguments.text: A stronger affirmative case would explicitly model evidential dependence. The hostile explanation may depend on the same tradition as the empty-tomb narrative, and bodily resurrection semantics may not independently prove a known burial place. The case should therefore ask whether its conclusion survives after correlated indicators receive reduced weight. If death, bodily absence, early proclamation, and sincere appearances still converge after that discount, the inference gains credibility precisely because it does not depend on counting every report as independent confirmation.

newArguments.title: Discriminating-predictions comparison
newArguments.text: Rather than claiming that every alternative fails, the affirmative could identify observations on which the accounts differ. Survival predicts a severely injured continuing Jesus and requires a pathway through custody; purely visionary accounts do not naturally predict bodily absence; pure literary development weakens expectations of a very early identified resurrection proclamation. None of those contrasts is decisive alone, but jointly they permit a transparent comparison. Resurrection earns preference only if it predicts the combined pattern with fewer unsupported auxiliary assumptions than each serious rival.

newArguments.title: Incremental-content audit
newArguments.text: The negative could separate the tradition into propositions and date the earliest secure support for each: Jesus died, God raised him, appearances were reported, the burial place was empty, and encounters involved tangible bodily interaction. Early support for the first three would not automatically backdate the final two. This incremental audit avoids treating every later detail as invention while still asking whether the evidence needed for physical resurrection appears only after additional narrative development. The motion fails if its distinctively physical components remain later or independently uncertain.

novelty.explanation: This introduces a proposition-by-proposition chronology rather than treating bodily tradition as one indivisible historical package.

newArguments.title: Likelihood-equivalence challenge
newArguments.text: The negative need not show that one naturalistic theory explains everything. It can ask whether crucial observations are approximately as expected under more than one account: sincere experiences under revelation or grief, early raising language under vindication, and increasing physical detail under clarification or development. Where rival accounts predict an observation comparably well, that observation contributes little discriminatory force. The affirmative must therefore identify evidence whose probability differs materially across the alternatives, rather than relying primarily on the number or vividness of mutually compatible facts.

novelty.explanation: This introduces a likelihood-based account of underdetermination that strengthens the burden analysis without adopting a single rival narrative.
